meta_title: Vikas Choudhary | Program Manager, Education & Development
meta_desc: Personal website of Vikas Choudhary, Program Manager at Pratham Education Foundation, Maharashtra. Thoughts, work, and writings on education, tribal schools, and social impact.
hero_bio_1: I'm a Program Manager at Pratham Education Foundation, working on a state-level initiative to improve learning outcomes in government tribal residential schools across Maharashtra. The program covers 500+ schools and involves everyone from Class 1 students learning to read their first word to government officials deciding how assessments get reported.
hero_bio_2: Most of what I do is unglamorous: reviewing data, visiting schools, troubleshooting implementation failures, and having the same conversations with teachers and superintendents until something actually changes. I find that more interesting than the version of this work that looks good in slide decks.
hero_bio_3: Before this I worked in STEM education and community outreach. Born in Bihar, educated in Haryana, and based in Delhi — I have a postgraduate degree in Hindi literature. This academic background turns out to be surprisingly useful in the field.
currently_text: Leading Year 3 of Majhi Shala, Majha Swabhimaan. We are focusing on midline assessments across 8,500+ students, Intense Catch-Up pilots in 36 schools, and building a live monitoring dashboard for 455+ Ashramshalas in Maharashtra.
work_intro: What I've been building, field-testing, and occasionally course-correcting.
work_1_desc_1: Majhi Shala, Majha Swabhimaan is a 3-year initiative to improve foundational learning outcomes in 500+ government tribal residential schools across four divisions of Maharashtra. I run the program, actively overseeing assessment design, teacher training, field team coordination, government liaison, and a live data dashboard for 455+ schools simultaneously.
work_1_desc_2: The hardest part isn't the scale. It's ensuring that what gets implemented on the ground actually matches what was designed. A training workshop is easy to run. The real challenge lies in getting 500 schools to change their teaching practices and systematically verifying those improvements.
work_2_desc: Designed and delivered technology education programs covering robotics, AI, block coding, and Scratch in schools that previously lacked these subjects. Also built the training content necessary for field teams and teachers to sustain the curriculum after my visits. The main difficulty was making these sessions genuinely engaging in classrooms with no reliable power supply and students who had never used a computer.
work_3_desc: Coordinated community awareness campaigns on public health and civic rights alongside local officials across the district. In parallel, I worked as a street theatre artist with Manthan Foundation. We used performance art to reach rural audiences often missed by conventional outreach strategies. This experience taught me that the most effective communication relies on meeting people exactly where they are.
work_4_desc: Ran the university's NSS unit: student volunteers, community projects, Unnat Bharat Survey, Swachh Bharat internship. My first real exposure to coordinating people toward a shared goal in conditions where nothing is guaranteed. More formative than it sounds.
writing_intro: Long-form pieces on education, program design, and what the field actually looks like. All opinions are my own.
blog_1_title: What 8,575 Assessments Taught Me About Learning Gaps in Tribal Schools
blog_1_excerpt: When our team completed midline assessments for over 8,500 students across ashram schools in Maharashtra, the data was both sobering and hopeful. Reading proficiency at the Story level jumped from 14% to 35%, marking a significant learning gain. However, the journey to achieve this revealed something far more important than any metric. The gap between what children are taught and what they actually understand is much wider than most program reports admit. Here's what I observed on the ground, and why honest assessment design is more important than building impressive dashboards.
blog_2_title: Why a Wooden Abacus Still Beats a Spreadsheet in the Classroom
blog_2_excerpt: I've seen a lot of education technology pitches for tablets, learning apps, and AI tutors. Yet some of my most memorable classroom moments from field visits to ashram schools in Amravati and Nashik involved a simple abacus, a set of 3D alphabet letters, and children who couldn't sit still because they were fully engaged in learning. Teaching Learning Materials (TLM) rarely get enough credit in policy conversations. This post explores what hands-on, activity-based learning looks like in practice, along with the specific teacher support required to sustain it.
blog_3_title: The Catch-Up Problem: Reaching Children Who Fell Behind Before We Arrived
blog_3_excerpt: A Class 6 student who cannot read a paragraph hasn't failed. Instead, the system successfully passed them along without ensuring foundational skills were built between Class 1 and now. The Catch-Up Course we've been rolling out across 500+ tribal residential schools in Maharashtra operates on a simple but radical premise: meet children exactly where they are rather than where the syllabus assumes they should be. Scaling this initiative across four divisions has taught me exactly what remedial education demands of teachers, field teams, and the institutions funding these programs.
thoughts_intro: Shorter reflections on the education and development sector — things I've been thinking about, questioning, or learning.
thought_1_text: "A child who can't read a paragraph by Class 6 isn't a slow learner. They are simply a student that the system moved forward without verifying foundation readiness. The core problem is structural rather than individual."
thought_2_text: "The most powerful teaching tool in a tribal school isn't a digital tablet. It's an educator who believes the child in front of them is capable of learning, backed by the proper skills and materials to make it happen."
thought_3_text: "We frequently discuss data-driven programs, but data is only ever as honest as the actual field conditions that produced it. Prioritize building genuine trust with your field teams first, and accurate numbers will naturally follow."
thought_4_text: "Scale without quality is just organized failure. The BOT model works only when what you're transferring is genuinely owned by the people who will sustain it."
